planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Wisley 2008 was introduced to mark an anniversary at the Royal Horticultural Society's Wisley garden.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Wisley 2008 bears clear pink, cupped double blooms with a light, fresh fragrance, opening on a vigorous, well-branched shrub bred with good disease resistance typical of more recent David Austin introductions. Its dependable, classic pink color and reliable garden performance have made it a popular general-purpose English rose. It reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall; prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain continued flowering.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Lady of Megginch Rose (Deep Crimson David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lady of Megginch bears deep crimson-red, rosette-shaped blooms on a vigorous, well-branched shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Lady of Megginch bears deep crimson-red, densely petaled, rosette-shaped blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, opening on a vigorous, well-branched shrub. Its rich, saturated color makes it a bold accent in a mixed border, especially paired with lighter pastel roses or perennials. It reblooms reliably from late spring through fall; prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain continued flowering.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Absolutely Fabulous Rose (Fragrant Golden-Yellow Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Absolutely Fabulous is a modern shrub rose bred for strong yellow color, fragrance, and improved disease resistance.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Absolutely Fabulous bears large, high-centered, golden-yellow double blooms with a notably strong, fruity fragrance, unusual for a modern landscape-type shrub rose bred primarily for disease resistance and repeat bloom. Its vigorous, well-branched habit and clean, glossy foliage give it a tidy garden presence between flushes, and it reblooms reliably through the growing season with good resistance to black spot and powdery mildew for easier care than many older yellow roses. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and prune moderately in late winter to shape the plant and remove any dead or crossing wood.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Distant Drums Rose (Unique Mauve-and-Apricot Bicolor Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Distant Drums is a Griffith Buck-bred shrub rose famous for its unusual smoky mauve-and-tan bicolor blooms and exceptional cold hardiness.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Distant Drums bears fully double blooms in an unusual, ever-shifting blend of tawny apricot-tan centers surrounded by smoky mauve-lavender outer petals, a color combination unlike almost any other rose and one that has made this Iowa State University-bred cultivar a cult favorite among collectors. Bred by Griffith Buck specifically for Midwestern hardiness, it tolerates cold winters and generally needs less spray intervention than older hybrid teas, growing on its own roots as a compact, own-root shrub. It reblooms through the growing season; deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and prune moderately in late winter to shape the plant.
sources: Iowa State University — Griffith Buck Rose Introductions
